ideas.build: Web app with a hosted voice cloning TTS API, text chunking, and audio stitching. Hardest part is consent and abuse prevention for voice cloning, plus chunk consistency.
ideas.demo_moment: Paste a bedtime story and hear it read in grandma's recorded voice.
ideas.post_hook: I made my own articles into audiobooks narrated by me.
ideas.risks: Voice cloning misuse; require a live read-aloud verification phrase.

evidence.summary: Qwen3 TTS's voice clone feature, run locally with a voice reference and text, was used to produce a custom audiobook.
Chaining Kokoro TTS with OpenVoice's tone color converter adds voice cloning to an existing TTS model for about 600 MB extra VRAM without retraining.
Cheap voice training and personal dictation models are being built to reduce post-transcription edits.

ideas.name: Commodity or Castle? Moat Builder
ideas.one_liner: A tiny strategy game where you run an AI lab and choose between racing on model quality, price cuts, or moving up the stack, while rivals commoditize you.
ideas.for_whom: MBAs, product people and business-curious readers who like case-study games.
ideas.why_it_works: The commoditization debate is a classic strategy question (moat vs commodity trap) with live market evidence. A game lets players feel the margin squeeze.
ideas.how_it_works: Over 8 quarterly turns, players pick actions (train a bigger model, cut price, launch a product, sign enterprise deals). Rival labs respond and margins/market share update. The end screen assigns a strategy archetype and a shareable scorecard.
ideas.build: React with a small rules engine, no backend; optional LLM for quarterly news flavor text. Hardest part: balancing the game so that multiple strategies are viable.
ideas.demo_moment: A quarter where you cut price 80% and the market-share bar leaps while the margin bar collapses.
ideas.post_hook: I built a game where you run an AI lab. 9 of 10 friends went bankrupt trying to race on price. Can you build a moat?
ideas.risks: Game balancing takes iteration; keep scope to 8 turns and 4 actions.

evidence.summary: Whether LLMs are becoming commodities: one side sees inference providers reallocating demand across models, the other sees brand and repeated model launches sustaining margins for labs.
Whether AI token demand will shift toward commodity models as intelligence per dollar rises, or stay split with a frontier tier, determines the economics of the market.
Whether AI labs can escape the commodity trap by moving up the stack into products and services, versus remaining undifferentiated model vendors with competition squeezing margins.
Whether frontier labs' pursuit of AGI is commercially justified or ideologically driven, with the claim that there is no real commercial case for LLM-based unstable systems.

ideas.name: Human Receipt
ideas.one_liner: A writing tool that records your drafting process and produces a verifiable 'written by a human' receipt page.
ideas.for_whom: Independent writers, students and Substack authors who need to prove their work is their own
ideas.why_it_works: Writers have trouble proving authorship, and detectors alone are unreliable. Process evidence (typing timeline, revisions) is a more convincing artifact.
ideas.how_it_works: User writes in a distraction-free editor that logs revision history and paste events. When finished, it generates a public receipt link showing a timeline, % typed vs pasted, and an optional AI-assistance disclosure.
ideas.build: React editor (TipTap) plus Supabase for event logs and a read-only share page. Hardest part: making the receipt credible without overclaiming; show the data, don't claim proof.
ideas.demo_moment: A time-lapse replay of an essay being written, appearing on a receipt page with a QR code.
ideas.post_hook: Nobody believes you wrote it yourself anymore. So I made a receipt.
ideas.risks: Can be gamed by retyping AI text; privacy of the draft history.

evidence.summary: Human writers face difficulty proving their work is their own now that AI can generate prose, making authorship verification a problem on writing platforms like Substack.
A tool or policy mechanism to distinguish or moderate AI-written content on discussion sites while preserving human-authored quality.
A tool to flag or report undisclosed AI-generated content on social feeds would address a gap users currently face.

ideas.name: Penny Router
ideas.one_liner: Type any task and see which AI model and effort level it deserves, then run it there and see what you saved.
ideas.for_whom: Professionals who pay for AI subscriptions or APIs and burn through limits on easy tasks.
ideas.why_it_works: Power users manually route work between cheap and strong models and tune thinking levels per task to stay inside limits. Nobody has packaged that judgment for non-engineers.
ideas.how_it_works: The user pastes a task. A small cheap model rates difficulty, stakes and needed reasoning. The app picks a tier (fast, balanced or deep), runs it, and shows a receipt such as 'Used the cheap model, saved about 80% versus always using the top model'. A override button reruns on the strong model.
ideas.build: Next.js or single-page app calling the OpenRouter API with 3 model tiers and a classifier prompt. Hardest part is making the difficulty classifier feel trustworthy and the cost math accurate.
ideas.demo_moment: Three tasks go in: a typo fix, a market analysis and a trivia question. Each is routed differently and a running 'saved $' counter ticks up.
ideas.post_hook: I stopped using the biggest AI model for everything. Here's the 30-second router I built and what it saved me.
ideas.risks: Misrouting hard tasks to weak models; model names and prices change often.

evidence.summary: Routing tasks across models by cost and specialization, using per-project instruction files to direct cheaper models for simple work and stronger models for hard work.
Routing tasks across multiple model vendors on the Pareto frontier is more valuable than single-vendor lock-in for coding work.
Users pick different GPT-5.6 models and thinking levels per task (Sol medium for building, background agents for hard tasks, Luna xhigh for daily productivity) to manage limits.
A user routes coding work across multiple agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build) via an Agentic Engineer bot with guidelines for picking the right tool per task.

ideas.name: Search Without the Summary
ideas.one_liner: A browser extension that hides AI Overviews on search pages and shows a ticker of how many publisher clicks that summary likely cost.
ideas.for_whom: People annoyed by AI summaries and bloggers or readers who care about publishers.
ideas.why_it_works: AI Overviews cut publisher traffic and sometimes make false claims, while the web fills with SEO slop. Users want control and a playful way to see the effect.
ideas.how_it_works: The extension collapses the AI summary box by default, replaces it with a 'Summary hidden, 7 sources below' banner, and keeps a tally of summaries dodged. Users can click to reveal and a weekly 'clicks returned to publishers' card is shareable.
ideas.build: Chrome extension (Manifest V3) with a content script and CSS selectors, local storage for counts. Hardest part: selectors breaking when Google changes markup.
ideas.demo_moment: Searching a question and watching the AI box fold away, with the counter incrementing.
ideas.post_hook: I hid Google's AI summaries for a week and sent 143 clicks back to real publishers. Here's the extension.
ideas.risks: Selector fragility; the 'clicks returned' number is an estimate and must be labeled so.

evidence.summary: Publishers like Stereogum report steep ad revenue losses after Google shifted search to AI Overviews, cutting traffic to their sites.
AI Overviews and AI Mode summaries reduce click-through traffic to publisher pages, hurting the ad revenue that funds the content being summarized.
AI Overviews produced false claims tying publishers to shady business practices, creating legal liability for search summaries.
Blogs and the open web are cluttered with AI-generated SEO content, pushing people to search forums like Reddit for genuine answers.

ideas.name: Soundtrack by Code
ideas.one_liner: Open a web page or doc and get a live-generated ambient soundtrack that reacts to what you do, from calm typing to rushed deadlines.
ideas.for_whom: Remote workers, students, game fans
ideas.why_it_works: Soundtracks generated through code instead of audio files, intensifying with action, show music can be adaptive and free.
ideas.how_it_works: User picks a vibe and the page runs a Web Audio synthesizer whose tempo and layers shift with typing speed or a timer. A slider shows the system adding layers as intensity rises.
ideas.build: Web Audio API or Tone.js with an LLM that writes the generator code per vibe. Hardest part is making it sound pleasant rather than noisy.
ideas.demo_moment: Type faster and watch drums and bass layers kick in.
ideas.post_hook: My focus music reacts to how fast I type.
ideas.risks: Music quality is subjective; offer 3-4 polished presets.

evidence.summary: Generating game soundtracks entirely through code instead of audio files, with music that intensifies as fighting breaks out.
Opus 5.5 generates a credible Bach-style fugue, which one musician found listenable for the first time from AI.

ideas.name: Parent Playlist Rescue
ideas.one_liner: A guided checker and migrator that helps parents lock down kid-unfriendly features and move playlists between music services.
ideas.for_whom: Parents of young kids using streaming apps
ideas.why_it_works: Parents disable Spotify's video feature or transfer playlists with scripts and cheap tools. The hack exists, but only as scattered tips and vibe-coded scripts.
ideas.how_it_works: Parent picks a service and sees a step-by-step settings checklist with screenshots. Optionally they paste a playlist link and the app builds a matching list for another service. A final 'kid-safe' score shows what is still open.
ideas.build: Static guide site with checklist state plus playlist-matching via public APIs. Hardest part is API approvals, so make the checklist the core and the migration optional via CSV exports.
ideas.demo_moment: A progress ring fills as each setting is toggled, ending with a green 'ready for the back seat' badge.
ideas.post_hook: One tiny setting changed what my kid sees on Spotify. I made a checklist for the rest.
ideas.risks: Settings change often; API restrictions from streaming services.

evidence.summary: Parents disable Spotify's video feature via the Videos and Canvas setting, or transfer playlists to another platform using cheap tools or vibecoded scripts.

ideas.name: Personal Canvas
ideas.one_liner: A drag-and-drop home page of widgets, such as todos, bookmarks and notes, that you describe in plain English.
ideas.for_whom: Professionals who want a custom dashboard without a Notion rabbit hole
ideas.why_it_works: Ben Tossell built a visual all-in-one dashboard and a personal canvas of widgets, and users build custom TV launchers. People want personal software shaped to them but not the code.
ideas.how_it_works: User types 'add a widget that shows my top 3 priorities and a countdown to launch'. The AI generates the widget on a canvas that they can drag around. Data is stored locally and the layout is shareable as a template.
ideas.build: React with a widget sandbox iframe, LLM generating widget HTML and localStorage. Hardest part is safe sandboxing and stable widget editing.
ideas.demo_moment: Describe a widget in a sentence and it appears on the canvas, working, in 5 seconds.
ideas.post_hook: I stopped searching for the right dashboard app and just describe widgets.
ideas.risks: Widget quality varies; competes with Notion and similar tools.

evidence.summary: Ben Tossell built a visual all-in-one dashboard combining todos, email, CRM, domains, and agent work logs so he and his agents can coordinate in one place.
Ben built a personal canvas of widgets pulling X bookmarks, emails, and todos, and had Codex generate a replacement for Loom after Loom's acquisition degraded it.
Users built custom TV launchers with Claude that personalize home screens and integrate with Home Assistant and Plex.

ideas.name: Pocket Arena
ideas.one_liner: Two phones in the same room battle in a mini browser game with no accounts, joined by a code or a sound.
ideas.for_whom: Friends, families and classrooms who want instant local multiplayer
ideas.why_it_works: Makers built browser RTS games with device-to-device multiplayer over an audio link and use WebSocket relays for multiplayer. Nobody has packaged zero-setup party games for non-developers.
ideas.how_it_works: Host picks a game template such as tug of war, reaction duel or word race. Friends join by scanning a QR code. The AI customises the theme, such as 'office edition', and the game starts.
ideas.build: Static site plus a small WebSocket relay on Cloudflare Workers; LLM only for themes and content. Hardest part is real-time sync, so keep the games turn-based or tap-based.
ideas.demo_moment: Scan a QR code on a second phone and both screens instantly turn into a head-to-head duel.
ideas.post_hook: I vibe-coded a multiplayer party game in an afternoon. Here is how the relay works.
ideas.risks: Real-time networking bugs; scope creep into too many games.

evidence.summary: Built a browser-based RTS game with Claude Opus 5.5 supporting device-to-device multiplayer over an audio link.
Developers use a vibe-coded WebSockets relay server to enable multiplayer in browser games.
Static hosting on GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages suits browser-based HTML/JavaScript vibe-coded games.

ideas.name: Weekend Dataset Maker
ideas.one_liner: Describe a niche collection you wish existed, and the app builds a browsable, shareable dataset page from public sources.
ideas.for_whom: Journalists, analysts, hobbyists and consultants who want a custom list or map
ideas.why_it_works: Makers built a film-discovery dataset, a map of lighthouses, and a dataset of open LLM mentions across 500K papers in a weekend. Non-coders want these artefacts but not the scripting.
ideas.how_it_works: User types a topic like 'every lighthouse you can visit in Maine'. The app searches the web, extracts structured rows, and shows an editable table plus a map or card view. User exports CSV or shares a public page.
ideas.build: Web app using LLM with web search tool, a table UI and Leaflet maps. Hardest part is accuracy and source citations, so show a source link per row and flag low-confidence entries.
ideas.demo_moment: Type one sentence and watch rows fill in live with pins appearing on a map.
ideas.post_hook: I built a dataset that did not exist, in 5 minutes, from one sentence.
ideas.risks: Hallucinated rows and scraping limits; needs clear sourcing.

evidence.summary: A user built a film-discovery dataset from a convenience set on plot.fyi, using AI to assemble a corpus that doesn't exist in full.
Mollick built a lighthouse map visualization by giving Claude Code plain-English instructions, showing non-coders can produce interactive tools this way.
Building a dataset of which open LLMs are mentioned across ~500K arXiv ML papers was done as a weekend project in under 72 hours using Codex.

ideas.name: Cap Clock
ideas.one_liner: A tiny dashboard where you log how fast you burn your AI chat limits and it predicts when you'll hit the wall.
ideas.for_whom: Heavy chatbot users on $20 plans who get cut off mid-project
ideas.why_it_works: Users get limits hit after minutes and no vendor shows a clear meter, so people rely on trial and error.
ideas.how_it_works: User taps 'I got capped' with the app, plan, and approximate time of day. Over time the app shows patterns ('You cap Gemini after ~25 messages') and suggests a fallback tool for the rest of the day. Anonymous aggregates show community-reported caps by plan.
ideas.build: Mobile-friendly web app, Supabase for logs, simple charts. Hardest part: cold-start data; seed with the user's own logs and make it valuable solo.
ideas.demo_moment: A countdown ring that says 'cap in ~42 minutes at your current pace' with a switch-to-backup suggestion.
ideas.post_hook: Nobody tells you how fast you're burning your AI limit. So I made a clock.
ideas.risks: Manual logging is a friction; crowdsourced data may be noisy.

evidence.summary: Users report Gemini Pro usage limits hitting 100% after about 8 minutes of chatting, despite a paid subscription.
Anthropic's subscription tier renaming and wording of weekly limits created confusion about whether effective Max usage quotas were reduced.
Agent usage limits on the $20 subscription tiers are consumed quickly, and heavier plans mainly buy more agent hours.

ideas.name: Handoff Slides
ideas.one_liner: Paste a list of URLs or notes and get a clean full-screen deck that you control from your phone.
ideas.for_whom: Speakers, teachers and anyone giving quick talks who hates slide tooling
ideas.why_it_works: Simon built a custom presentation app that turns a list of URLs into slides remote-controlled from his phone, and Nathan Lambert built a markdown-native slides tool. A web version for non-developers is missing.
ideas.how_it_works: User pastes links or markdown. The app builds slides with screenshots and AI-written talking points. A QR code opens a phone remote with notes and next/prev buttons.
ideas.build: Web app with markdown to slides, screenshot API, and a WebSocket remote. Hardest part is reliable URL screenshots and cross-device sync.
ideas.demo_moment: Scan the QR code, swipe on your phone, and the laptop deck changes with your notes visible on the phone.
ideas.post_hook: I stopped making slides. I paste links and present from my phone.
ideas.risks: Competes with existing deck tools; screenshot rights and quality.

evidence.summary: Built a custom macOS SwiftUI presentation app, remote-controlled from a phone, to turn a list of URLs into full-screen slides.
Built a markdown-native slides tool for academics that works with agents, after investing hundreds of hours learning to make slides with agents.
Nathan Lambert built an agent-native slides tool for academics that builds to HTML/PDF with code, math, bibliography, and charts, and is seeking early testers.

ideas.name: Offline Pocket Oracle
ideas.one_liner: A fully in-browser decision helper that weighs your options using a small local model, with nothing leaving your device.
ideas.for_whom: Privacy-minded professionals and anyone facing small daily decisions
ideas.why_it_works: There is demand for fast, cheap in-browser decision models, and local models in the browser are now practical.
ideas.how_it_works: User types a choice such as two job offers or dinner options and sets what matters. A WebGPU local model scores each option and shows probability bars with a short reasoning line. A 'privacy: nothing sent' badge stays visible.
ideas.build: WebLLM or Transformers.js in a static page with a small model. Hardest part is model download size, load time and getting stable numeric scoring.
ideas.demo_moment: Turn on airplane mode and it still ranks your options.
ideas.post_hook: An AI decision helper that works in airplane mode.
ideas.risks: Small model quality and WebGPU support vary; frame it as a thinking aid.

evidence.summary: Users want fast, cheap in-browser decision or option-probability models for quick judgments without generating text.
Mirai lets users run local models directly in the browser.
Running a 1.7B on-device model with 256K context fits in about 1GB at 4-bit, enabling local agents on small hardware.

ideas.name: Open vs Closed Race Track
ideas.one_liner: A little racing game where a closed-model car leads by months and an open-weight car keeps catching up; tweak the 'gap' and watch the race.
ideas.for_whom: Curious non-technical readers who've heard 'open models are six months behind' but don't get why it matters.
ideas.why_it_works: The open-closed gap is a recurring, quantified debate (4-6 months, widening vs converging). A race metaphor makes the stakes tangible.
ideas.how_it_works: User picks 'gap dynamics' (converging, constant, widening) and a price lever. The race animates over several 'model release' laps and a caption explains who wins which task categories. Result card summarizes what that world looks like for users.
ideas.build: HTML canvas or simple CSS animation with JS timers. Hardest part: making the metaphor accurate and not just cute.
ideas.demo_moment: The open car draws level at the final lap just as the closed car launches a boost.
ideas.post_hook: Is open-source AI catching up or falling behind? I made a race where you set the rules and watch.
ideas.risks: Metaphor may oversimplify; keep captions grounded in the debate.

evidence.summary: Open-closed model gap debate: whether open models will always lag closed frontier models or are converging, with data showing a 4-6 month gap.
Open-weight models trail closed frontier models by roughly six months, and the gap may persist unless training dynamics change or open builders run out of money.
Whether the gap between frontier closed labs and open source models is widening because ideas compound over time.
Whether GLM-5.2 is near frontier parity with Mythos (rebutted as nonsense) versus being a strong but clearly behind open model.

ideas.name: Token Price Time Machine
ideas.one_liner: Type a task and see what it would have cost with frontier AI over the past year as prices dropped, rose, or got quietly changed.
ideas.for_whom: Curious professionals and AI-budget owners who can't tell whether AI is getting cheaper or pricier.
ideas.why_it_works: Price cuts, hikes, and plan changes are contested and confusing: cheaper models, 80% cuts, rising frontier prices. A simple timeline makes the confusion legible.
ideas.how_it_works: User picks a typical task ('summarize 50-page PDF', 'draft 100 emails') and sees a timeline of what it costs on a budget vs frontier model with annotated events. A toggle shows the 'if subsidies end' scenario.
ideas.build: React with a hand-curated JSON of model prices and events plus Chart.js. Hardest part: keeping price data accurate and sourced; label as approximate.
ideas.demo_moment: Selecting a task and watching two lines diverge as an annotated 80% price cut drops one of them.
ideas.post_hook: The same AI task cost $4 last year and 12 cents now. Or did it? Here's the time machine.
ideas.risks: Data maintenance burden and accuracy; scope to a few models.

evidence.summary: Whether OpenAI's 80% price cut on GPT-5.6 Luna reflects a market-capture push or a fundamental cost breakthrough is unresolved.
Frontier closed model prices keep rising for the smartest models, pushing AI buyers' unit economics higher.
Opus 5.5's 40% cheaper claim is contested: some say cost and speed gains are negated by usage and by cheaper rival models, while others see it as a real win on price.
Many AI application startups depend on subsidized inference, making their business models fragile if API pricing normalizes.

ideas.name: Vibe Game Jam Arena
ideas.one_liner: A showcase site where people submit AI-built mini-games and everyone plays and votes in 60-second rounds.
ideas.for_whom: Vibe coders, game fans and casual players
ideas.why_it_works: Simon Willison noted that vibe-coded games are now fun but that traditional game jams don't fit, and wants new ways to compare them.
ideas.how_it_works: Creators paste a link or HTML file and a prompt-used note. Players get a random game for 60 seconds, then rate it on fun and originality. A leaderboard and badges show the top builds each week.
ideas.build: Next.js with Supabase for submissions and votes, sandboxed iframes. Hardest part is moderating and sandboxing arbitrary user HTML safely.
ideas.demo_moment: Swipe through a feed of tiny games, each playable instantly.
ideas.post_hook: A game jam where every entry took under an hour to build.
ideas.risks: Moderation burden and cold start; seed it with your own games.

evidence.summary: New avenues or competitions for vibe game developers to compare and showcase their projects, since traditional game jams may not suit them.
Simon Willison argues vibe-coded games have reached an inflection point where they are actually fun to play.
Interest in a no-AI filter on Steam, reflecting demand for distinguishing vibe-coded games from legitimate indie projects.

ideas.name: What Was I Doing Yesterday
ideas.one_liner: A browser extension that quietly logs tabs and summarises your day into a recap you can ask questions of.
ideas.for_whom: Busy knowledge workers who lose context between days
ideas.why_it_works: A developer built a daemon that logs activity and answers 'what was I doing yesterday'. Non-developers have the same pain with tabs and docs, and local-first logging is attractive.
ideas.how_it_works: Install the extension, which stores page titles and time spent locally. At end of day it creates a three-bullet recap and an open-loops list. User asks 'where was that pricing page?' and gets the link.
ideas.build: Chrome extension with IndexedDB and an LLM call on titles only, user-supplied key. Hardest part is privacy defaults, so exclude domains and keep everything local.
ideas.demo_moment: Ask 'what was that article about pricing I read Tuesday?' and the link pops up instantly.
ideas.post_hook: My browser now remembers my week better than I do.
ideas.risks: Privacy sensitivity and extension store review; browser history already exists.

evidence.summary: A developer built a daemon that logs shell, editor, and Claude activity, summarizes it with Haiku, stores it in SQLite, and exposes it via MCP to answer 'what was I doing yesterday'.
An HN user built a personal MCP service that lets any AI chat save structured data, auto-generating schemas and Kanban, timeline, and calendar views.

ideas.name: Text Adventure Skin
ideas.one_liner: Load a classic text adventure and play it with a friendly GUI that has maps, inventory and optional hints.
ideas.for_whom: Nostalgic gamers and newcomers who find parsers intimidating
ideas.why_it_works: Users built a Codex interface for the open-sourced A Mind Forever Voyaging, in original or easier form. Interactive fiction has many open classics, and a generic skin would widen the audience.
ideas.how_it_works: User picks an open-source interactive fiction title from a shelf. The app runs it in a web interpreter and adds clickable verbs, an auto-map and hint levels. An optional AI narrator rewrites the prose in a chosen style.
ideas.build: Web app embedding a Z-machine interpreter such as Parchment with an overlay UI. Hardest part is parsing the game state for maps and inventory.
ideas.demo_moment: Click a verb instead of typing and a map draws itself as you walk through rooms.
ideas.post_hook: I made a 1980s text adventure playable for people who never touched a parser.
ideas.risks: Licensing of games; only open-source titles.

evidence.summary: Users built an interface using Codex to play the open-sourced text adventure A Mind Forever Voyaging in original or easier GUI form.
Simon Willison argues vibe-coded games have reached an inflection point where they are actually fun to play.
